title: Group 7: halogens
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT05#t4 term and clue written for the game; PT05#t2 term and clue written for the game; PT05#t3 term and clue written for the game; PT05#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: PT05#N.3, PT05#N.7, PT05#N.11, PT05#N.16.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Bleach
items.clue: Solution of sodium chlorate(I), made from chlorine and cold dilute NaOH.

items.label: Oxidising agent
items.clue: Role of Cl₂ when it takes electrons from Br⁻ or I⁻ and is itself reduced.

items.label: Disproportionation
items.clue: The same element is both oxidised and reduced in one reaction, as chlorine is with water.

items.label: London forces
items.clue: Attractions between molecules arising from temporary induced dipoles; stronger with more electrons.

questions.stem: At room temperature iodine is a solid but chlorine is a gas. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The I–I covalent bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond, so iodine molecules are harder to break up.
Iodine molecules have more electrons, so the London forces between them are stronger.
Iodine molecules are polar, so permanent dipole–dipole forces hold them together.
Iodine is more electronegative, so each molecule attracts its neighbours more strongly.

questions.explanation: I₂ has 106 electrons and Cl₂ has 34. Larger temporary dipoles form, so the intermolecular forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

questions.stem: Bromine water is added separately to aqueous potassium chloride and to aqueous potassium iodide. Which observation is expected?

options.text: A reaction occurs with the potassium chloride only
There is no reaction with either of the two solutions
A reaction occurs with both of the salt solutions
A reaction occurs with the potassium iodide only

questions.explanation: Bromine oxidises iodide ions, which are below it in Group 7: Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), and the solution darkens to brown. Bromine cannot oxidise chloride ions.

questions.stem: In which reaction is chlorine both oxidised and reduced?
questions.explanation: One Cl atom goes from 0 to −1 (reduced) in HCl; the other goes from 0 to +1 (oxidised) in HClO. That is disproportionation.

questions.stem: Swimming pools are often disinfected by adding a white solid, Ca(ClO)₂, instead of chlorine gas. Why does it kill bacteria in the same way as chlorine does?

options.text: It releases chloride ions, which are toxic to bacteria even at low concentrations.
Its calcium ions are taken up by bacteria and stop their cells from dividing.
It gives chlorate(I) ions, the oxidising agent that chlorine forms in water.
It slowly releases chlorine gas, which kills the bacteria as it bubbles out.

questions.explanation: Ca(ClO)₂ is calcium chlorate(I). Dissolved, it gives ClO⁻ ions, which form HClO in water. These are the oxidising agents that kill bacteria, just as when Cl₂ reacts with water (Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO).
